subject: VPC/on-prem scaling math for sustained + spiky inference loads
messages:
From: Samir Desai <samir.desai@acme.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
Cc: Acme Procurement <procurement@acme.com>
Date: 2028-07-19T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: On-prem sizing question — peak bursts and steady queries

Hi Lauren,

Quick context: we're evaluating a Private deployment (VPC) for our inference stack. Typical steady-state is ~120 requests/minute for the large model path, but we have 3–4 business events a week that spike traffic for ~15–30 minutes to roughly 40x.

Primary asks: can Redwood's private offer sustain the steady baseline with predictable latency while also absorbing short high-magnitude bursts without re-provisioning GPUs mid-event? We need:
- a back-of-envelope sizing recommendation (how many GPUs for steady vs peak)
- an explanation of how autoscale + cache-warmup behaves during spikes
- a note on network egress and NVLink / host networking constraints if we add more GPUs to the node

We can share logs and a synthetic trace if helpful. Goal is a procurement spec we can hand to our infra team.

Thanks,
Samir
Samir Desai
Head of Infrastructure, Acme Corp

From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
To: Samir Desai <samir.desai@acme.com>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>, Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-19T11:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: On-prem sizing question — peak bursts and steady queries

Samir — thanks for the clear brief. We can definitely design for sustained baseline + burst buffering without manual reprovisioning. Attaching a quick workbook with our assumptions (capacity_model.xlsx). High-level answers below, then Rishi will share the worked math.

Summary (short):
- Baseline (120 req/min ~ 2 req/sec): 1 x A40-equivalent GPU can handle the steady path if requests are batched and average token length is modest.
- Burst headroom: to cover 40x spikes (~80 req/sec) we recommend a two-tier approach: reserved baseline + a warm burst buffer of pre-warmed instances that can take ~10–20s to ramp to full KV cache hit rates. That typically maps to 4–6 GPUs as hot buffer depending on model size.
- Autoscale behavior: our private runtime supports async pre-warming (start VMs with container warm-up hooks) and shadow traffic to keep KV cache fragments hot. Autoscale alone will add capacity in ~30–90s depending on provisioning method; warm buffers reduce user-facing tail latency during that window.
- Networking: main constraint is link saturation during model parameter sync and large offloads (checkpoint loads). Recommend 100GbE between host fabric for multi-GPU nodes. If your topology uses cross-rack traffic for KV syncing, factor in 1–2x headroom.

Next steps: Rishi will post the worked numbers in-thread; if this aligns, we can schedule a short call with your infra team and our deployment engineer to walk the topology (I included a Drive link).

- Lauren

Attachments: capacity_model.xlsx
From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>, Samir Desai <samir.desai@acme.com>
Cc: Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya.rao@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-19T13:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: On-prem sizing question — peak bursts and steady queries (worked math)

Adding the math we used in the attachment and inline for quick review. Assumptions: model = 30B parameters (quantized), avg response = 120 tokens, avg tokens/sec per GPU = ~400 (sustained streaming), desirable p99 latency < 300ms.

Worked sketch (back-of-envelope):
- Steady: 120 req/min = 2 req/sec. If we do small batching (batch size ~2–4), one GPU can serve ~200–400 sync-inference requests/sec depending on caching; even conservatively counting 100 req/sec capacity -> 1 GPU more than covers baseline.
- Peak (40x): 80 req/sec. To hit p99 <300ms without cold-cache penalty, aim for effective capacity ~160 req/sec (2x headroom). So required GPUs = ceil(160 / 100) = 2 GPUs if cache warm. But cold-start/warm-up behavior can temporarily double latency, so we recommend a hot buffer of 4 GPUs to be safe for the 15–30 minute spikes.
- Autoscale policy suggestion: keep baseline reservation = 1 GPU, warm buffer (standby) = 3 GPUs with pre-warmed containers; scale-up cap = +5 GPUs on emergency. Warm buffer uses lightweight shadow traffic (~1–2qps per GPU) to keep next-token KV shards hot.

Networking and IO: model parameter fetch on container start ~12–18GB; with 100GbE a cold start copy across nodes is ~1–2s per 10GB ignoring storage overhead, but orchestration and container start add latency. If you rely on cross-rack fetching for shards, multiply by number of shards.

I've attached capacity_model.xlsx which contains the per-GPU throughput curve and a sensitivity tab.

- Rishi

Subject: Re: On-prem sizing question — peak bursts and steady queries

Thanks Rishi — helpful. A couple clarifying Qs before we turn this into an infra spec:
1) How much additional NIC bandwidth should we reserve per node to avoid tail latency during the 40x bursts (assuming 100GbE fabric)?
2) For the warm buffer you recommend, do we need dedicated VMs (wasted reservation) or can we use a spot-like preemptible pool that you keep warm via our shadow traffic?
3) Any suggested SLOs for model reload failures during a spike (we want a fallback path to a smaller replica with graceful degradation).

We have a short window tomorrow afternoon for a call if you can do 30 minutes. Also procurement wants the likely monthly committed baseline + burst buffering estimate to place in the PO.

Samir
From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
To: Samir Desai <samir.desai@acme.com>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya.rao@redwood.com>, Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-20T14:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: On-prem sizing question — peak bursts and steady queries (next steps + topology)

Samir — answers inline then propose next steps.

1) NIC headroom: reserve ~25–30% headroom on 100GbE for model shard fetches + KV sync during bursts. Practically that's ~75–80Gb/s usable. If you expect multi-node cross-rack fetches, increase to 40% headroom.

2) Warm buffer funding model: we offer two options: (A) dedicated warm standby (reserved VMs) — simplest, predictable cost; (B) preemptible pool with continuous lightweight shadow traffic that keeps containers warm. Option B reduces committed cost but requires your infra to accept occasional preemptions; we can design a fallback routing policy. For procurement, we'll show both numbers in the workbook.

3) Suggested SLOs for reload failures: target <1% per-week reload failure and <5s degraded latency window on graceful fallback to a smaller replica. We recommend an automatic fallback model (smaller quantized variant) with a documented quality delta.

Attached is a rough topology diagram (network_topology.png) and a one-pager on SLA/bursting options (sla-bursting-notes.pdf).

If that looks good, let's lock a 30-minute call tomorrow 15:00–15:30 PDT. I'll invite our deployment engineer (Aditya) to cover orchestration details.

Thanks,
Lauren

Attachments: network_topology.png, sla-bursting-notes.pdf
